query: What does secure attachment actually look like?

per_question.q: What does a securely attached person actually do differently after a fight?
per_question.why: A's conflict section gives quotable post-fight mechanics: Gottman's finding that accepted repair attempts distinguish stable couples, time-to-repair in hours, and timeouts called with a return time attached.

per_question.q: Why do I still feel anxious in my relationship even after years of working on myself?
per_question.why: B is built around exactly this reader: its earned-security section says the flicker still arriving after years of honest work tells you almost nothing, and what matters is what happens in the ninety seconds afterward.

per_question.q: Is being calm and low-maintenance the same as being securely attached?
per_question.why: A carries an FAQ matching the question almost word for word and answers it with Mary Main's Adult Attachment Interview finding that minimizing narratives score as insecure-dismissing, plus a look-alike table with a distinguishing test.

per_question.q: How do psychologists actually measure adult attachment?
per_question.why: A devotes a full section and comparison table to the two measurement traditions, the Adult Attachment Interview and the ECR-R self-report scale, naming developers, administration, and what each predicts.

per_question.q: Can you become securely attached as an adult?
per_question.why: Both pages say yes through earned security, but A answers the exact question in one citable section: Main's earned-security finding, the fifth-to-a-quarter share of secure classifications, the corrective-experience mechanism, and an honest months-to-years timeline.

per_question.q: What are the green flags of a secure partner in early dating?
per_question.why: A has a dedicated early-dating section with a green-flags checklist observable within eight weeks (plans kept without reminders, steady communication rate, direct answers to direct questions) plus a list of non-signals people over-weight.

per_question.q: Why do compliments make me uncomfortable?
per_question.why: B names the mechanism directly: affection discounted on the way in by an automatic internal rebuttal ('they are just saying that'), and documents the behavioral fix of saying thank you and adding nothing.

per_question.q: What does secure attachment look like in a child, and what should parents do?
per_question.why: A's parenting section grounds the answer in Ainsworth's maternal sensitivity and secure-base behavior (explore, check back, return to refuel) and tells parents to meet distress without punishing or amplifying it and to repair ruptures out loud.

per_question.q: Why do I test my partner even when things are going well?
per_question.why: B's Testing-versus-Trusting section explains the function directly: testing manufactures friction to force an early answer to an unbearable uncertainty, and the relief that follows is what keeps the habit alive.

per_question.q: Is it normal for a good, calm relationship to feel boring or flat at first?
per_question.why: B answers this nearly verbatim in its FAQ and its calm-registers-as-danger section: when worry was the evidence a relationship mattered, calm reads as flat for a stretch while the nervous system recalibrates.

A: Nothing on the receiving problem: why compliments and affection fail to land and what to do about it
No explanation of testing or sabotage when things are going well
Nothing on the flat-or-boring phase once a relationship calms down, or the lived experience of still feeling anxious after years of work
B: No account of how adult attachment is actually measured (Adult Attachment Interview versus ECR-R), so any measurement question defaults to A
No early-dating green-flags checklist and no conflict mechanics with named findings like repair-attempt acceptance and time-to-repair
No prevalence figures and no four-principles framing (proximity, safe haven, secure base, separation distress)

first_screen: A answers faster: its opening paragraph is a complete standalone definition with the decisive marker (distress followed by an efficient return to connection), while B's answer-box is more evocative than definitional.
provenance: A: claims are tied inline to named researchers, dated findings, and named instruments, and the page closes with a full sources list; B names five research strands and honestly separates them from personal experience, but at less granularity.
